newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Duke's reputation sinks 60 years after abdication.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Duke's reputation sinks 60 years after abdication.

text.p: Sixty years after he gave up the throne of England to marry American divorcee Wallis Simpson, the late Duke of Windsor's reputation has sunk to a new low.
Secret government papers covering the years of World War Two released this month show clearly that he was selfish Nazi sympathiser lacking in the most elementary political sense.
One document dating from July 1940 makes clear that the Germans expected him the take over as king if they won the war.

"The Germans expect assistance from the Duke and Duchess of Windsor, the latter desiring at any price to become queen. The Germans have been negotiating with her since June 27," said the memo detailing the views of a secret service informant.

Another paper among those released for the first time by Britain's Public Record office shows the duke thought "the age of constitutional monarchy had passed, evidently believing the age of Fuehrers such as Petain, Franco and Salazar had opened".
The duke, who met Nazi leader Adolf Hitler in 1937, was not guilty of treason in the strictest sense.
But the official papers illustrate a pattern of pro-German behaviour in the darkest days of the war that would almost certainly have put anyone who was not a former king behind bars for a long time.
BACKGROUND TO ABDICTION
Few in Britain in 1936 were aware of the imminent abdication, the first by a British monarch in nearly 600 years, because people could only read about it in newspapers imported from Europe.
The British press maintained a deferential conspiracy of silence on the affair between King Edward VIII and the twice divorced Wallis Warfield Spencer Simpson from Baltimore.
When the situation was announced in the British press and parliament on December 3, 1936, the king had to move fast.

Within a week he had signed the abdication documents. On December 11 the abdication was ratified by parliament and the following day Edward's brother Bertie became king, taking the title King George VI.
Edward became the His Royal Highness the Duke of Windsor and married Wallis Simpson in June 1937.
The new king refused to give her a royal title too, a decision that laid the groundwork for a mass of bad feeling between the duke and the rest of his family.

And if the abdication was a probably the worst blow to the British monarchy this century, the duke's future behaviour did nothing to improve the situation as far as the government and many of the British people were concerned.
"The embarrassments caused to the king by the Duke and Duchess of Windsor were to be almost limitless," said historian Robert Rhodes James, writing in the Daily Express.

When France fell in 1940, the duke and duchess fled from their villa at Antibes to Madrid and British wartime prime minister Winston Churchill tried unsuccessfully to persuade them to return to England.

The duke was unwilling to come back to London if he and his wife were to be accorded "different status" from the rest of the royal family. Churchill was not amused and despatched a stiff telegram to the former king.

"Your Royal Highness has taken active military rank. Refusal to obey direct orders of competent military authority would create a serious situation. I hope it will not be necessary for such orders to be sent," Churchill said.
In the end, it was decided to send the duke to the Bahamas to take up the post of colonial governor, which he held until 1945.
The foreign secretary Lord Halifax wrote to Sam Hoare, British ambassador in Madrid: "I dare say it is quite a good plan that they should go the Bahamas, but I am sorry for the Bahamas."

Despite having to fight the Germans, the government in London was soon inundated with requests from the duke for large sums of money to redecorate his official residence and for permission to leave his post and travel to New York.
Churchill was particularly keen for the duke not to go to the United States, where he was likely to attract adverse publicity.

The duke also had to be warned against giving press interviews harmful to British interests after he suggested to the American magazine Liberty, at a time when Churchill was trying to bring the United States into the war, that Washington would be better off staying out.

An angry Churchill sent a telegram to the duke, saying: "Whatever was meant, the language will certainly be seen as defeatist and pro-Nazi and, by implication, approving the isolationist aim of keeping America out of the war.
"I could wish indeed that your Royal Highness would seek advice before making public statements of this kind."

An anonymous British government official was more damning about the man who had once been king, saying, according to one file: "The Duke of Windsor is notoriously pro-Nazi. He is also a heavy drinker and what few wits he had have wilted."
